# Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, First Part

## Statement

Let $f$ be a real function which is continuous on the closed interval $[a,b]$ (with $a<b$).
Let $F : [a,b] \to \mathbb R$ be defined by
$$F(x) \;=\; \int_a^x f(t)\,\mathrm dt .$$
Then $F$ is a primitive of $f$ on $[a,b]$; that is, $F$ is differentiable at every $x\in[a,b]$ (one‑sidedly at the endpoints) and
$$F'(x) = f(x)\qquad\text{for all } x\in[a,b].$$

The claim is true, and we prove it.

## 0. Conventions and the definitions used

**Integral.** We use the Darboux integral (equivalent to the Riemann integral). For $u<v$ and $g$ bounded on $[u,v]$, a *partition* of $[u,v]$ is a finite set $P=\{u=t_0<t_1<\dots<t_n=v\}$, and
$$L(g,P)=\sum_{i=1}^n m_i\,(t_i-t_{i-1}),\qquad U(g,P)=\sum_{i=1}^n M_i\,(t_i-t_{i-1}),$$
where $m_i=\inf_{[t_{i-1},t_i]}g$ and $M_i=\sup_{[t_{i-1},t_i]}g$. The lower and upper integrals are
$\underline{\int_u^v} g=\sup_P L(g,P)$ and $\overline{\int_u^v} g=\inf_P U(g,P)$; $g$ is *integrable* on $[u,v]$ when these agree, and their common value is $\int_u^v g$. We also set $\int_u^u g=0$.

**Derivative at an endpoint.** For $x\in[a,b]$, "$F'(x)=c$" means
$$\lim_{h\to 0,\; h\neq 0,\; x+h\in[a,b]} \frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h} = c ,$$
i.e. for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $\bigl|\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}-c\bigr|\le\varepsilon$ for every $h\neq0$ with $|h|<\delta$ and $x+h\in[a,b]$. At $x=a$ only $h>0$ occurs and at $x=b$ only $h<0$ occurs, so this is the usual one‑sided derivative there. (Since $a<b$, for each $x\in[a,b]$ there are admissible $h$ of arbitrarily small modulus, so the limit is meaningful.)

**Primitive.** $F$ is a *primitive of $f$ on $[a,b]$* iff $F$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ in the above sense and $F'=f$ there.

## 1. Preliminary lemmas

Throughout, $g$ denotes a **bounded** real function on a closed interval $[u,v]$ with $u<v$; recall $m_i,M_i$ are the infimum and supremum of $g$ on the $i$‑th subinterval of the partition, which are finite because $g$ is bounded.

### Lemma 0 (Basic Darboux facts)
Let $g$ be bounded on $[u,v]$, $u<v$.

1. If $P\subseteq P'$ are partitions of $[u,v]$ ($P'$ *refines* $P$), then
 $$L(g,P)\le L(g,P')\qquad\text{and}\qquad U(g,P')\le U(g,P).$$
2. For **any** two partitions $P,Q$ of $[u,v]$: $\;L(g,P)\le U(g,Q)$.
3. Consequently $\underline{\int_u^v}g$ and $\overline{\int_u^v}g$ are finite and
 $$L(g,P)\;\le\;\underline{\int_u^v}g\;\le\;\overline{\int_u^v}g\;\le\;U(g,P)\qquad\text{for every partition }P. \tag{1.1}$$
 In particular, if for some $P$ one has $U(g,P)-L(g,P)<\varepsilon$, then $0\le\overline{\int}g-\underline{\int}g<\varepsilon$.

*Proof.*

**(1)** By induction on the number of points of $P'\setminus P$ it suffices to treat $P'=P\cup\{c\}$ with $c\notin P$, say $t_{i-1}<c<t_i$. Write $m'=\inf_{[t_{i-1},c]}g$, $m''=\inf_{[c,t_i]}g$. Since $[t_{i-1},c]$ and $[c,t_i]$ are subsets of $[t_{i-1},t_i]$, we have $m'\ge m_i$ and $m''\ge m_i$, so
$$m'(c-t_{i-1})+m''(t_i-c)\;\ge\;m_i(c-t_{i-1})+m_i(t_i-c)=m_i(t_i-t_{i-1}).$$
All other terms of $L(g,P)$ and $L(g,P')$ coincide, so $L(g,P')\ge L(g,P)$. The statement for $U$ is symmetric ($\sup$ over a subset is $\le$ the $\sup$, giving $U(g,P')\le U(g,P)$).

**(2)** For any partition $R$ one has $L(g,R)\le U(g,R)$, because $m_i\le M_i$ termwise and the subinterval lengths are positive. Applying this to the common refinement $R=P\cup Q$ and using (1) twice,
$$L(g,P)\le L(g,P\cup Q)\le U(g,P\cup Q)\le U(g,Q).$$

**(3)** By (2), every lower sum is a lower bound for the set of upper sums and every upper sum is an upper bound for the set of lower sums; both sets are non‑empty. Hence $\underline{\int}g=\sup_P L(g,P)$ is finite and $\le$ every $U(g,Q)$, so taking the infimum over $Q$, $\underline{\int}g\le\overline{\int}g$, and $\overline{\int}g$ is finite. The outer inequalities in (1.1) are immediate from the definitions of $\sup$ and $\inf$. $\blacksquare$

### Lemma 1 (Continuous $\Rightarrow$ integrable)
If $g$ is continuous on $[u,v]$ with $u<v$, then $g$ is bounded on $[u,v]$ and integrable there.

*Proof.* $[u,v]$ is closed and bounded, hence compact, so a continuous $g$ on it is bounded (extreme value theorem) and, by the Heine–Cantor theorem, uniformly continuous.

Let $\varepsilon>0$. Pick $\eta>0$ with $|g(s)-g(t)|<\dfrac{\varepsilon}{2(v-u)}$ whenever $s,t\in[u,v]$, $|s-t|<\eta$. Choose $n\in\mathbb N$ with $(v-u)/n<\eta$ and let $P$ be the partition into $n$ equal subintervals $[t_{i-1},t_i]$ of length $(v-u)/n$. On each $[t_{i-1},t_i]$ the continuous function $g$ attains its supremum $M_i$ and infimum $m_i$ (extreme value theorem), say at $s_i,r_i$; since $|s_i-r_i|\le (v-u)/n<\eta$,
$$M_i-m_i=g(s_i)-g(r_i)<\frac{\varepsilon}{2(v-u)} .$$
Hence
$$U(g,P)-L(g,P)=\sum_{i=1}^n (M_i-m_i)\frac{v-u}{n}\le \frac{\varepsilon}{2(v-u)}\cdot (v-u)=\frac\varepsilon2<\varepsilon .$$
By Lemma 0(3) this gives $0\le \overline{\int_u^v}g-\underline{\int_u^v}g<\varepsilon$, and since $\varepsilon>0$ was arbitrary the upper and lower integrals coincide: $g$ is integrable. $\blacksquare$

Since a restriction of a continuous function is continuous, Lemma 1 applies to $f$ on every subinterval $[u,v]\subseteq[a,b]$. In particular $\int_a^x f(t)\,\mathrm dt$ exists for every $x\in[a,b]$ (for $x=a$ it is $0$ by convention), so **$F$ is well defined**.

### Lemma 2 (Additivity over adjacent intervals)
Let $u\le w\le v$ in $[a,b]$. Then
$$\int_u^v f=\int_u^w f+\int_w^v f .$$

*Proof.* If $w=u$ or $w=v$ this is trivial (one term is $0$ by convention). So assume $u<w<v$; all three integrals exist by Lemma 1.

Let $\varepsilon>0$. By the Darboux criterion (the computation in Lemma 1 applied on $[u,w]$ and on $[w,v]$) choose partitions $P_1$ of $[u,w]$ and $P_2$ of $[w,v]$ with
$$U(f,P_i)-L(f,P_i)<\varepsilon/2 \quad (i=1,2).$$
Then $P=P_1\cup P_2$ is a partition of $[u,v]$ containing $w$, and directly from the definitions (the subintervals of $P$ are exactly those of $P_1$ together with those of $P_2$),
$$L(f,P)=L(f,P_1)+L(f,P_2),\qquad U(f,P)=U(f,P_1)+U(f,P_2).$$
Now, by (1.1) applied on $[u,v]$ with the partition $P$,
$$L(f,P_1)+L(f,P_2)=L(f,P)\le \int_u^v f\le U(f,P)=U(f,P_1)+U(f,P_2),$$
and, by (1.1) applied on $[u,w]$ with $P_1$ and on $[w,v]$ with $P_2$, $L(f,P_1)\le\int_u^w f\le U(f,P_1)$ and $L(f,P_2)\le\int_w^v f\le U(f,P_2)$; adding,
$$L(f,P_1)+L(f,P_2)\;\le\;\int_u^w f+\int_w^v f\;\le\; U(f,P_1)+U(f,P_2).$$
Both numbers $\int_u^v f$ and $\int_u^w f+\int_w^v f$ therefore lie in an interval of length $U(f,P_1)+U(f,P_2)-L(f,P_1)-L(f,P_2)<\varepsilon$, whence
$$\Bigl|\int_u^v f-\Bigl(\int_u^w f+\int_w^v f\Bigr)\Bigr|<\varepsilon .$$
As $\varepsilon>0$ was arbitrary, the two are equal. $\blacksquare$

### Lemma 3 (Crude bounds from the trivial partition)
Let $u<v$ in $[a,b]$, and put $m=\inf_{[u,v]}f$, $M=\sup_{[u,v]}f$ (finite by Lemma 1). Then
$$m\,(v-u)\;\le\;\int_u^v f\;\le\;M\,(v-u).$$

*Proof.* Let $P_0=\{u,v\}$ be the trivial partition. Then $L(f,P_0)=m(v-u)$ and $U(f,P_0)=M(v-u)$, and by Lemma 0(3) (inequality (1.1)) together with integrability of $f$ on $[u,v]$ (Lemma 1),
$$m(v-u)=L(f,P_0)\le\underline{\int_u^v}f=\int_u^v f=\overline{\int_u^v}f\le U(f,P_0)=M(v-u).\qquad\blacksquare$$

## 2. Proof of the theorem

Fix $x\in[a,b]$ and let $\varepsilon>0$.

**Continuity at $x$.** Since $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, it is continuous at $x$ relative to $[a,b]$: there is $\delta>0$ such that
$$t\in[a,b],\ |t-x|<\delta \;\Longrightarrow\; |f(t)-f(x)|<\varepsilon. \tag{2.1}$$

Now let $h\neq0$ satisfy $|h|<\delta$ and $x+h\in[a,b]$. Write
$$I_h=\bigl[\min(x,x+h),\,\max(x,x+h)\bigr]\subseteq[a,b],$$
a closed interval of length $|h|>0$. Every $t\in I_h$ satisfies $|t-x|\le|h|<\delta$, so by (2.1)
$$f(x)-\varepsilon\;\le\; f(t)\;\le\; f(x)+\varepsilon \qquad\text{for all } t\in I_h. \tag{2.2}$$
Consequently, with $m_h=\inf_{I_h}f$ and $M_h=\sup_{I_h}f$,
$$f(x)-\varepsilon\le m_h\le M_h\le f(x)+\varepsilon. \tag{2.3}$$

**Step 1: the increment of $F$ is an integral over $I_h$.**

*Case $h>0$.* Then $a\le x<x+h\le b$ and $I_h=[x,x+h]$. Lemma 2 with $u=a,\ w=x,\ v=x+h$ gives
$$F(x+h)=\int_a^{x+h}f=\int_a^{x}f+\int_x^{x+h}f=F(x)+\int_{I_h}f,$$
so $F(x+h)-F(x)=\int_{I_h}f$ and, since $h=|h|$,
$$\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}=\frac1{|h|}\int_{I_h}f. \tag{2.4}$$

*Case $h<0$.* Then $a\le x+h<x\le b$ and $I_h=[x+h,x]$. Lemma 2 with $u=a,\ w=x+h,\ v=x$ gives
$$F(x)=\int_a^{x}f=\int_a^{x+h}f+\int_{x+h}^{x}f=F(x+h)+\int_{I_h}f,$$
so $F(x+h)-F(x)=-\int_{I_h}f$; since $h=-|h|$,
$$\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}=\frac{-\int_{I_h}f}{-|h|}=\frac1{|h|}\int_{I_h}f. \tag{2.5}$$

So in **both** cases
$$\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}=\frac1{|h|}\int_{I_h}f . \tag{2.6}$$

**Step 2: estimate.** Applying Lemma 3 on $I_h$ (length $|h|>0$) and dividing by $|h|>0$:
$$m_h\;\le\;\frac1{|h|}\int_{I_h}f\;\le\;M_h .$$
Combining with (2.3) and (2.6),
$$f(x)-\varepsilon\;\le\;\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}\;\le\;f(x)+\varepsilon,$$
that is,
$$\left|\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}-f(x)\right|\;\le\;\varepsilon \tag{2.7}$$
for every admissible $h$ with $0<|h|<\delta$.

**Conclusion.** Since $\varepsilon>0$ was arbitrary and $\delta$ was produced from it, (2.7) says precisely that
$$\lim_{h\to0} \frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}=f(x),$$
the limit being taken over $h\neq0$ with $x+h\in[a,b]$. Hence $F$ is differentiable at $x$ (one‑sidedly if $x=a$ or $x=b$) with $F'(x)=f(x)$.

As $x\in[a,b]$ was arbitrary, $F$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ with $F'=f$, i.e. $F$ is a primitive of $f$ on $[a,b]$. $\blacksquare$

## 3. Remarks

1. Differentiability implies continuity, so $F$ is in particular continuous on $[a,b]$.
2. Global continuity of $f$ entered only through Lemmas 1–3 (existence of the integrals, additivity, and the crude bounds); the argument of Step 2 itself used continuity of $f$ only *at the point $x$*. Since additivity and the bounds of Lemma 3 hold for any Riemann‑integrable function (with the same proofs, the Darboux criterion replacing Lemma 1), it follows that for a merely Riemann‑integrable $f$ the function $F$ is differentiable at every point of continuity of $f$, with derivative $f(x)$ there.
3. The use of the "$\le\varepsilon$" form of the limit definition is harmless: if $|q_h-c|\le\varepsilon$ holds for all $0<|h|<\delta(\varepsilon)$ and all $\varepsilon>0$, then given $\varepsilon'>0$ apply this with $\varepsilon=\varepsilon'/2$ to get $|q_h-c|\le\varepsilon'/2<\varepsilon'$.
